doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Independent revolution and learning the record business
summary: Owning the label meant no one else to blame; they learned radio, promotion and distribution around the dining room table.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. Sort of like saying, “Oh I can’t blame my bad saxophone playing on my reed anymore.”

Right. Right. So we worked 24 hours — we were so excited I think that the new adventure, the autonomy gave us so much energy, being on our own and to make it happen. So we would lose a lot of sleep thinking about how we were going to do things. Because we didn’t know how to do things. We learned, we had a desire to do something but we had to learn the mechanics of it, the infrastructure. We had to learn about that. What makes the — how can I get the music to the marketplace? What makes it successful? Radio stations — we had to talk about radio stations and program directors who deal with program directors and traffic.
I’m guessing between the record label and the magazine that your dining room table was usually covered with papers and business?

Yeah. And everybody — the dining room table was where it’s at. It all happened at the dining room table. People would come in from all over the world and we’d sit at the dining room table. You know? And figure stuff out. Have meetings and stuff like that. And I’ve still got the dining room table, still, it’s happening today, 55 years later it’s still going on.
